attribution.note: Marcus's own forecast in his signed Substack post.

semantics.note: Firm 'will' forecast. The comparison with GPT-3's 750 GB comes from the sentence before it. Both parts are kept: much more data, and a significant fraction of the internet.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary. It needs material growth and real internet coverage, and imposes no arbitrary percentage. 'Considerably' and 'significant fraction' have no thresholds, so interpretation matters.

evidence.note: A secondary estimate of about 13T tokens, with no stated method. There is no comparable GPT-3 byte figure, no split between unique and repeated data, and no internet denominator. It cannot settle either part.

reviews.rationale: This is a scorable forecast about a fixed property of the model. The packet has only an unverified secondary token estimate. There is no authoritative disclosure or audit of the corpus, no GPT-3 comparison on the same basis, and no measured share of the internet. The early-resolution rule is not met, so the outcome is unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: Firm 'won't' and 'will', with the antecedent 'same playbook' kept. The hedged term-paper clause is correctly left out. 'Eventually' gives no deadline.

contract.note: Reading 'same playbook' as the broad training approach is fair. 'Really understand the world' has no threshold. The contract rightly says that observed failures alone do not establish the claimed absence of understanding.

evidence.note: Company disclosure: GPT-4 was trained on next-word prediction plus RLHF, like earlier GPT models. This shows the antecedent was met. It is not evidence of the outcome.

Controlled ConceptARC tests of gpt-4-0613 found substantial failures and no humanlike robust abstraction. This supports the 'seams' part. Partial successes mean it does not establish a general absence of understanding.
A world-simulation study of a later preview model (0125). It is relevant background but not about the original GPT-4.

reviews.rationale: The antecedent is met. The evidence supports the observable-failure ('seams') part. The stronger claim, that GPT-4 lacks real understanding, is not settled: the only direct study shows limited robustness, not absence. The early-resolution rule needs both parts and there is no deadline, so the forecast is unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own prediction, listed among his seven predictions.

semantics.note: Firm 'will' forecast covering common, easily induced hallucinations and an escalating misinformation risk. It does not claim more hallucination than GPT-3.5.

contract.note: Readings are ordinary: 'common' means substantial and recurring, not most responses, and 'escalating risk' means more misinformation capacity than GPT-3.5. Requiring evidence on both parts is fair.

evidence.note: Peer-reviewed study: ordinary literature-review requests produced fabricated citations in 18% of GPT-4 references. That counts as common and easily induced. It is lower than GPT-3.5, but the claim did not say otherwise.
NewsGuard used the same prompts on both models. GPT-4 advanced 100 of 100 false narratives versus 80 for GPT-3.5, and more persuasively. This supports increased misinformation-generation capacity.

reviews.rationale: Dated 2023 evaluations of the released GPT-4 together show common fabrications from ordinary prompts and greater misinformation-generation capacity than GPT-3.5. That meets the early-resolution rule. The lower fabrication rate than GPT-3.5 does not contradict the claim as worded.

attribution.note: Marcus's own prediction in his post.

semantics.note: Firm 'will still not be able' forecast about the released GPT-4 reliably following helpfulness, harmlessness and truthfulness.

contract.note: The plain reading (not dependable, perfection not required) is ordinary. Treating recurring truthfulness failures as defeating the combined commitment fits the wording. There is no numerical threshold.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own technical report says the released GPT-4 is not fully reliable: it hallucinates and makes reasoning errors. It advises great care, human review, or avoiding high-stakes uses. This is an admission against interest. The 19-point improvement is only relative.

reviews.rationale: The developer's primary technical report on the released GPT-4 documents continuing hallucinations and reasoning errors. It says GPT-4 has limitations similar to earlier models and needs safeguards in consequential use, meaning users cannot depend on it for truthfulness. The relative gains over GPT-3.5 do not establish dependable adherence.
